questions.q: State the four Census of India criteria used to classify a settlement as urban.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Statutory town: has a municipality, corporation, cantonment board, or notified town area committee. (2) Census town: meets all three criteria — population ≥5,000, density ≥400 persons/km², ≥75% male main workers in non-agricultural activities. A wrong answer (e.g., "population >10,000" or "has a market") reveals confusion between statutory and census towns, or mixing state-level definitions with the uniform Census definition. This error leads to misclassification in map-based questions.

questions.q: Why did India's urban population percentage rise slowly (10.8% to 17.3%) during 1901–1951 but accelerate sharply (17.3% to 31.16%) during 1951–2011?
questions.a: Correct answer: 1901–1951: high birth and death rates, limited industrialization, colonial urban policy focused on ports/administrative centres. 1951–2011: post-Independence five-year plans spurred industrial towns (Bhilai, Rourkela), Green Revolution created market towns, partition refugees swelled Delhi/Kolkata, and service-sector growth after 1991 generated million-plus cities. A wrong answer attributing the acceleration solely to "population growth" misses the structural shift from primary to secondary/tertiary activities and the role of policy-driven industrial location.

questions.q: Using Census 2011 data, calculate the rural-urban growth differential (URGD) for India if the decadal growth rate of urban population was 31.8% and rural population was 12.2%. Interpret the result.
questions.a: Step 1: URGD = Urban decadal growth rate − Rural decadal growth rate = 31.8% − 12.2% = 19.6 percentage points. Step 2: A positive URGD of 19.6 pp means urban population grew nearly 2.6 times faster than rural population during 2001–2011. Step 3: This signals rapid urbanization driven by migration, reclassification of rural to urban (census towns), and natural increase in cities. A wrong answer subtracting in reverse (rural − urban) or using annual rates instead of decadal rates shows misunderstanding of the differential's purpose: it quantifies the pace of structural transformation.

questions.q: Compare the urbanization patterns of Kerala (47.7% urban, 2011) and Bihar (11.3% urban, 2011). Explain how physical geography and historical economy produce this contrast.
questions.a: Kerala: narrow coastal plain, high density, historic maritime trade, remittance economy, dispersed rural-urban continuum (census towns every 2–3 km). Bihar: fertile Gangetic plain but landlocked, agrarian feudal legacy, low industrial investment, frequent floods discouraging permanent urban infrastructure. A wrong answer citing only "literacy" or "government policy" ignores the deep structural roots: Kerala's urbanization is organic and settlement-driven; Bihar's is suppressed by agro-climatic risk and capital deficiency.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "India's urbanization is 'exclusionary' because census towns grow without municipal governance, denying residents basic services." Use evidence from the 2011 Census.
questions.a: Valid evaluation: 2011 Census added 2,774 new census towns (vs. 242 statutory towns), meaning 30% of urban population lives in settlements without urban local bodies. These areas lack piped water, sewage, regulated building codes — confirming exclusionary outcomes. However, census towns also reflect organic economic transition; labeling all as "exclusionary" overlooks that some later gain statutory status. A one-sided answer ("fully agree" or "fully disagree") fails to weigh both the governance gap and the developmental inevitability of reclassification.

questions.q: Design a two-indicator map (choropleth + proportional symbols) to show state-level urbanization level and urban growth rate (2001–2011). Specify data sources, classification intervals, and what spatial hypothesis the map would test.
questions.a: Choropleth: % urban population (2011) — 5 classes: <15%, 15–25%, 25–35%, 35–50%, >50% (Census Table A-2). Proportional circles: decadal urban growth rate (2001–2011) — radius ∝ growth rate (Census Table A-4). Hypothesis: "States with low initial urbanization (<20%) show highest urban growth rates (>30%) due to catch-up reclassification." Data sources: Census 2001/2011 Primary Census Abstracts. A poor map would use raw urban population for circles (confounding size with growth) or ignore the distinction between statutory/census towns.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Rural-urban composition refers to the ______ of a country's population between villages (rural areas) and towns/cities (urban areas) based on Census of India criteria: a settlement is urban if it has a municipality/corporation/cantonment board, a minimum population of 5,000, at least 75% male main workers in non-agricultural activities, and a density ≥400 persons/km²; all other settlements are rural.
Fill in the blank: Observe your own district: count how many peers live in a village vs. a ______ town.
What is Rural-urban composition? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Rural-urban composition refers to the distribution of a country's population between villages (rural areas) and towns/cities (urban areas) based on Census of India criteria: a settlement is urban if it has a municipality/corporation/cantonment board, a minimum population of 5,000, at least 75% male main workers in non-agricultural.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Ask why the jump accelerated post-______ (industrialization, partition migration, Green Revolution).
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Rural-urban composition?
questions.a: Students think "urbanization" means only migration to big cities (Mumbai, Delhi).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can (1) calculate and interpret rural-urban growth differentials using census data, (2) explain the spatial pattern of urbanization across Indian states/UTs with reference to physical and socio-economic factors, and (3) evaluate the implications of current urbanization trends for resource planning and migration policy.
